questions.q: What is the difference between visible and invisible design?
a: Visible design is what customers see; invisible design is how you deliver it
Visible design is the logo; invisible design is the advertising budget
Visible design is for staff; invisible design is for customers
Visible design changes yearly; invisible design never changes
questions.why: Lesson 1 says visible design covers products and branding, while invisible design covers processes and culture.

questions.q: What did Coca-Cola learn before redesigning its Minaqua water bottle?
a: Japanese buyers valued recycling and lived in small homes
Japanese buyers wanted larger bottles for families
Bottled water was losing ground to soft drinks
Customers preferred glass bottles over plastic
questions.why: Lesson 1 shows research shaping a small, stackable, recyclable bottle.

questions.q: When should a startup shift from flexible to stable?
a: Once it has found a strong product-to-market fit
As soon as it hires its first employee
Before it has tested any version of the product
Only after it has expanded into several countries
questions.why: Lesson 2 says startups must stay flexible until they find fit, then standardize to scale.

questions.q: What stayed essentially unchanged at Coca-Cola for over 90 years?
a: The bottle design, font, color and franchise model
The recipe, price and advertising agency
The company's ownership and headquarters
The target market and distribution countries
questions.why: Lesson 2 says those core design elements gave Coca-Cola a stable, recognizable identity.

questions.q: How does Coca-Cola's open innovation system work?
a: Customers experiment within fixed tools and contribute product ideas
Outside agencies are paid to file patents for the company
Employees compete privately for research budgets
The company buys promising startups and absorbs their teams
questions.why: Lesson 3 describes the Design Machine, where templates are fixed but the rest is open, saving $100 million.
